title: Boundary-Aware Evidence Selection for Robust RAG
one_liner: When a model retrieves facts to answer questions, it should pick evidence that is challenging enough to teach the model something real, not passages that either hand over the answer or remain too confusing.
lead: Retrieval-Augmented Generation is when a model first searches a knowledge base for relevant facts, then uses those facts to answer a question—like looking up a recipe before you cook. But today's search systems pick facts based only on how closely they match the question, often grabbing passages that are either too simple or too hard for the model to learn from. BAR-RAG picks evidence based on the generator's actual needs: passages that are just hard enough to teach the model, without being impossible.

problem.h2: Why today's retrieval picks the wrong evidence
paras: Consider answering a trivia question: Is a tomato a fruit or a vegetable? A naive search engine might return passages that say the answer directly (a fruit), or passages that are completely off-topic. In both cases, the model learns nothing—when the passage gives away the answer, the model takes a shortcut instead of reasoning; when the passage is too confusing, there are no real clues to follow. The model needs a middle ground: a passage that is genuinely challenging to reason through but contains enough real clues to reach the right answer.

Today's retrievers and rerankers (the systems that pick which facts to use) optimize only for relevance to the question. They rank passages by how well they match the keywords, not by whether the passage will actually teach the generator something. This leaves the generator fragile: when retrieval is noisy or imperfect, the model struggles because the wrong kind of evidence was chosen.

callout.html: Evidence selection ignores what the generator needs to learn, picking passages that hide the answer or fail to teach it.

steps.text: Search the knowledge base, get back many candidate passages ranked by keyword match.
For each passage, test the generator on it alone: does the generator succeed, and how much effort did it require?
Pick passages where the generator found the task challenging but succeeded—not trivial, not impossible.
Fine-tune the answer-model on this curated evidence, teaching it to reason over challenging passages.
At test time, use the trained model with the same evidence-selection strategy, so it handles imperfect retrieval.

paras: The reranker—the system that scores and picks which passages to use—shifts from optimizing for relevance alone to optimizing for a passage's ability to teach the generator. Instead of ranking passages by keyword match, it ranks them by whether they give the generator a real learning challenge.

hidden.h2: The Goldilocks Zone: challenge level without failure
hidden.name: Learning challenge—difficulty and solvability
paras: The hidden quantity is a passage's learning value: how much real reasoning does the generator have to do when using this passage, and does the passage contain enough information to actually reach the right answer? A trivial passage—one that gives the answer away—has zero learning challenge. A broken passage—one with misleading or incomplete information—has challenge but no solvability. The sweet spot is passages where the generator must think hard but can succeed with the available clues.

The paper measures this by using generator feedback: for each candidate passage, run the generator on just that passage alone, see if it gets the answer right, and measure how uncertain or mistaken it was along the way. Passages where the generator struggled but ultimately found the right answer are highest-value. The reranker learns to score passages by this signal instead of by keyword relevance.

heat.caption: Darker passages teach the model more. Highlight (marked) shows the Goldilocks passages: challenging and solvable.

reads.html: A passage is valuable if using it alone makes the model work hard but still get the right answer.
The reranker learns to maximize the generator's test-time performance on passages it selects, which biases selection toward evidence in the Goldilocks Zone—neither trivial nor unsolvable.

mechanism.h2: Why choosing the right evidence makes models handle noise better
paras: The mechanism has two parts. First, the reranker is trained with reinforcement learning: for each candidate passage, it measures how well the generator answers using only that passage, and adjusts the reranker's scores to rank high-learning passages highest. This creates a feedback loop where the reranker learns to spot evidence that is genuinely useful for reasoning, not just keyword-relevant. Passages that force the generator to think but contain real clues get high scores; passages that either hide the answer or provide misleading clues get low scores.

Second, the generator is fine-tuned on the curated set of passages the reranker selected. In normal training, the generator might see passages that are too easy (answer is obvious) or too hard (no real clues). By training only on passages where the generator struggled but succeeded, the model learns to reason more carefully over evidence. It becomes attuned to real clues and genuine reasoning chains, so at test time—when retrieval is noisy and imperfect—the model has already practiced handling evidence that is genuinely challenging. It no longer relies on shortcuts like word-matching or surface patterns that break when irrelevant passages appear.

stages.s: Question and retrieved passages ranked by keyword match
Test: generator tries each passage alone
Measure: success and difficulty of each attempt
Reranker learns to score by challenge and solvability
Fine-tune generator on curated Goldilocks evidence
Trained model that reasons over challenging evidence, handles noisy retrieval

math.words: For each passage, use reinforcement learning to adjust its reranker score based on how well the generator performs using only that passage. Train the generator on passages that maximize its test-time accuracy under realistic noise.
math.equation: L_reranker = - sum_i r(p_i) * log(score(p_i)) where r(p_i) is generator accuracy on passage p_i
symbols: the reranker's probability that passage i is useful
reward: does the generator get the right answer using passage i alone?
the reranker's loss to minimize—negative because we maximize reward

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Passage A (trivial): Generator scores 100% correct, but no challenge. reward = 0.5 (low learning value).
Passage B (challenging-and-right): Generator scores 85% correct with reasoning. reward = 1.0 (high learning value).
Passage C (misleading): Generator scores 30% correct. reward = 0.2 (fails to teach).
Reranker learns: boost score(B) highest, then A, then C. Generator trains on B and improves overall reasoning.

math.note: Reward measures the generator's actual performance with each passage—higher reward means the passage gives a real learning signal.

charts.title: Naive reranking by relevance
charts.note: When retrieval is noisy, picking passages by keyword match fails because irrelevant passages dominate.

charts.title: BAR-RAG boundary-aware selection
charts.note: Models trained on challenging-but-solvable evidence drop less than 10% when retrieval includes wrong passages.

items.html: To measure if a passage lets the generator answer correctly, you need the right answer. At test time you do not have it. The paper assumes access to correct answers during training, which works for fixed knowledge bases but fails if questions evolve or answers change.

items.b: Generator feedback is noisy early in training.
items.html: At the start of training, the generator is weak and gives unreliable feedback. A passage might look hard-but-doable simply because the generator is untrained, not because the passage is genuinely useful. This chicken-and-egg problem means early reranker training can mislearn.
Testing the generator on each candidate passage requires multiple forward passes. With thousands of passages and millions of questions, this is slow and may not scale to real-time retrieval.

Use a curriculum: start with rough relevance ranking, gradually refine scores as the generator improves—because early feedback is noisy, gentle updates prevent mislearning. Batch passage evaluation to amortize computation. Cache results across similar questions.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple question-answering system with five questions and a small knowledge base of twenty passages. First, show that naive passage selection (picking by keyword match) breaks under simulated retrieval noise: when you add irrelevant passages to the mix, accuracy drops. Then run BAR-RAG: for each passage, feed it to the answer model alone and measure performance. Score passages high if the model succeeded despite the passage being challenging. Fine-tune the answer model on these high-scoring passages. Finally, re-run with noisy retrieval: show that BAR-RAG-trained models maintain accuracy where naive models fail.
demo.metric_eq: robustness = accuracy_under_noise - accuracy_clean_baseline. Goal: robustness > 5%, which means retrieval noise causes less than 5% absolute drop.
demo.closing: The key visual proof: a bar chart showing accuracy across clean and noisy retrieval, with BAR-RAG shrinking the performance gap where naive methods collapse.
